cards.body: Denormalizing everything up front. Start normalized, measure the hot query, then denormalize that path and decide how copies stay in sync (same transaction, events, or accepted staleness).

questions.prompt: An order history page joins orders, products and sellers on every view and is now the slowest query. Most reasonable first change?

choices.label: Copy product and seller names into the order rows for that page
Move all data to a document store
Drop the foreign keys
Denormalise every table in the schema

questions.explanation: Fix the measured hot path; keep the rest normalised.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of copying the seller name into 10M order rows?

choices.label: Reads need more joins
The database loses ACID
A seller rename must update many rows, or the copies go stale
Orders can no longer be indexed

questions.explanation: Denormalising moves cost from reads to writes.

questions.prompt: Which data should stay normalised?

choices.label: The seller name on a cached order page
Account balances that must never disagree with themselves
The product name printed on old invoices
The author name on comment listings

questions.explanation: One copy means it cannot disagree with itself.

questions.prompt: Order the recommended process.

items.label: Decide how copies stay in sync

questions.explanation: Denormalise late and on purpose.

questions.prompt: Show product names on order history: copy or join?
constraints: Order history is the hottest page
Old orders should show the name at purchase time

approaches.label: Copy the name into the order row
approaches.description: One-row reads

approaches.label: Join the live product table
approaches.description: Always current

rationaleOptions.label: Keeping the name as it was at purchase is actually wanted
The hottest page becomes a one-row read
Copied names can never go stale

rationaleConflicts.r3: They can. Here staleness is acceptable, even wanted, but you still decide how renames propagate.

questions.explanation: Copying suits read-heavy pages whose data rarely changes.

flashcards.back: Update anomalies: the same fact stored in two places disagreeing.
Faster reads for extra writes and the work of keeping copies in sync.
After a measured hot read path, with a clear sync strategy.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

title: Transactions & ACID
objectives: Explain each ACID property with an example
Show how atomicity protects a transfer
Spot code that needs a transaction

cards.title: ACID
cards.body: Atomicity: all of a transaction’s writes happen or none do. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other’s half-done work. Durability: once committed, the change survives a crash.

cards.title: Atomicity in practice
cards.body: A transfer debits one account and credits another. If the server crashes between the two, atomicity rolls the debit back, so money never disappears in between.

cards.title: A transfer transaction
cards.body: 5 steps from “BEGIN” to “COMMIT (or ROLLBACK on error)”, via “Read both balances”.
steps: Write the change to the log

cards.title: Durability
cards.body: Commit returns only after the change is in the write-ahead log on disk, and with synchronous replication on a replica too. After a crash the database replays the log.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Running two related writes as separate auto-committed statements. A crash between them leaves half a change. Put them in one transaction, and keep it short.

questions.prompt: Inside one transaction, the server crashes after debiting A but before crediting B. After restart?

choices.label: The database asks the user what to do
Neither change is visible: the transaction rolled back
Both changes are applied because the debit started
A is debited and B is not

questions.explanation: All or nothing.

questions.prompt: Which ACID property guarantees a committed order survives a power cut?

choices.label: Atomicity
Consistency
Durability
Isolation

questions.explanation: Committed means written to the log.

questions.prompt: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint stops a transfer from overdrawing. Which property is that?

choices.label: Consistency
Durability
Isolation
Atomicity

questions.explanation: Constraints that hold before and after every transaction.

questions.prompt: Order a transfer transaction.
questions.explanation: The log write is what makes commit durable.

questions.prompt: Two related writes run as separate auto-committed statements. What can go wrong?

choices.label: Reads become slower
A crash between them leaves only half the change
The second write is always rejected
They deadlock every time

questions.explanation: One transaction makes them atomic.

flashcards.front: Inside one transaction, the server crashes after debiting A but before crediting B. After restart?
flashcards.back: Neither change is visible: the transaction rolled back. All or nothing.

flashcards.front: Which ACID property guarantees a committed order survives a power cut?
flashcards.back: Durability. Committed means written to the log.

flashcards.front: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint stops a transfer from overdrawing. Which property is that?
flashcards.back: Consistency. Constraints that hold before and after every transaction.

flashcards.front: Two related writes run as separate auto-committed statements. What can go wrong?
flashcards.back: A crash between them leaves only half the change. One transaction makes them atomic.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

title: Isolation Levels
objectives: Name the anomalies each isolation level prevents
Pick a level for money vs analytics
Explain why stronger isolation costs throughput

cards.title: What isolation protects
cards.body: Concurrent transactions can see each other’s half-done work. Isolation levels decide which anomalies you accept: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and write skew.

cards.title: The levels
cards.body: Read committed: no dirty reads (Postgres default). Repeatable read / snapshot: a stable view for the whole transaction. Serializable: as if transactions ran one at a time, at the cost of more aborts and retries.

cards.title: Two doctors go off call
cards.body: 4 steps from “Both read: 2 doctors on call” to “Serializable aborts one transaction”, via “Each removes themselves”.
steps: Snapshot isolation lets both commit: 0 on call

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Assuming the default level is serializable. Most databases default to read committed, so check what you are getting before relying on it for money.

questions.prompt: Which anomaly does READ COMMITTED prevent?

choices.label: Phantoms
Non-repeatable reads
Dirty reads
Write skew

questions.explanation: It only hides uncommitted data.

questions.prompt: Two on-call doctors each check “someone else is on call” and remove themselves, under snapshot isolation. Result?

choices.label: One blocks until the other commits, so one stays on call
Snapshot isolation always serialises them
Both commit and nobody is on call (write skew)
Both are rolled back automatically

questions.explanation: Each saw a consistent snapshot; together they broke the rule.

questions.prompt: Order these isolation levels from weakest to strongest.
questions.explanation: Stronger levels allow fewer anomalies and cause more aborts.

questions.prompt: Isolation for a seat-booking transaction.
constraints: Many users race for the same seats

approaches.label: Serializable, with retries on abort
approaches.description: As if one at a time

approaches.label: Repeatable read / snapshot
approaches.description: Stable view per transaction

approaches.label: Read committed (the default)
approaches.description: No extra cost

rationaleOptions.label: Aborted transactions can be retried safely
Serializable rejects interleavings such as write skew
Snapshot isolation prevents write skew

rationaleConflicts.r3: Snapshot gives a stable view but still allows write skew, as in the doctors example.

questions.explanation: Pay for serializable where an invariant spans rows.

questions.prompt: A Postgres app relies on serializable behaviour without setting it. What does it actually get?

choices.label: Read committed, the default
Snapshot isolation for writes only
Read uncommitted
Serializable, the default

questions.explanation: Check the level before relying on it for money.

flashcards.back: Read committed.

flashcards.front: What anomaly can snapshot isolation still allow?
flashcards.back: Write skew.
More aborts and retries, lower throughput under contention.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

title: BASE & Eventual Consistency
objectives: Explain what BASE trades away
State what eventual consistency guarantees and what it does not
Choose a conflict resolution strategy

cards.title: BASE
cards.body: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. Instead of locking replicas together, the system keeps answering and lets replicas catch up in the background. Reads may be stale for a while.

cards.title: What “eventual” guarantees
cards.body: If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value. It does not say how soon, and it does not stop a user seeing an older value after a newer one.

cards.title: A like on a post
cards.body: 5 steps from “User taps like” to “Replicas converge”, via “Nearest replica accepts the write”.

cards.title: Resolving conflicts
cards.body: Two replicas may accept conflicting writes. Last-write-wins keeps the later timestamp and silently drops the other; counters and sets can merge instead (CRDTs); some apps keep both versions and ask the user.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using eventual consistency for a wallet balance. Two replicas can both approve a spend. Keep money and inventory on strongly consistent paths.

questions.prompt: Under eventual consistency, what is guaranteed?

choices.label: Reads never go backwards in time
Every read returns the latest write
Replicas converge within 100 ms
If writes stop, replicas converge to the same value

questions.explanation: Convergence, with no time bound.

questions.prompt: Which feature suits BASE-style eventual consistency?

choices.label: Wallet debits
Like counts on posts
Seats for a sold-out show
Claiming a unique username

questions.explanation: A briefly stale like count harms nobody.

questions.prompt: Two replicas accept different edits to a profile bio. With last-write-wins, what happens?

choices.label: The edit with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently lost
The user is asked to choose
Both edits are merged character by character
The write is rejected until replicas agree

questions.explanation: LWW is simple but drops data.

questions.prompt: Order an eventually consistent write.
questions.explanation: The reply comes before replication finishes.

questions.prompt: Count video views at a million increments a second.

approaches.label: One strongly consistent counter row
approaches.description: Exact, single location

approaches.label: Per-replica counters merged in the background (a CRDT counter)
approaches.description: No coordination on write

rationaleOptions.label: This gives exact real-time counts everywhere
Per-replica counters merge without coordination
A slightly stale count is acceptable

rationaleConflicts.r3: Counts converge later; viewers may see an older number for a while.

questions.explanation: Mergeable counters scale writes when exactness can wait.

flashcards.front: Under eventual consistency, what is guaranteed?
flashcards.back: If writes stop, replicas converge to the same value. Convergence, with no time bound.

flashcards.front: Which feature suits BASE-style eventual consistency?
flashcards.back: Like counts on posts. A briefly stale like count harms nobody.

flashcards.front: Two replicas accept different edits to a profile bio. With last-write-wins, what happens?
flashcards.back: The edit with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently lost. LWW is simple but drops data.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

title: Replication
objectives: Copies of data on multiple nodes for availability and read scaling; sync vs async trade-offs.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Leader-follower: writes to leader, replicas serve reads with lag. Sync replication = no loss but slower; async = fast but may lose recent writes on failover. Multi-leader adds conflict resolution.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Copies of data on multiple nodes for availability and read scaling; sync vs async trade-offs.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Write to leader” to “Reads from replicas”, via “Leader logs change”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Reading your own write from a lagging replica — the user sees their order "missing". Use read-your-writes routing.

questions.prompt: A user posts a review, refreshes, and it is missing. Likely cause?

choices.label: A database constraint rejected it silently
The read went to a replica that had not caught up yet
The user’s session expired
The leader lost the write

questions.explanation: Route a user’s reads to the leader briefly after they write.

questions.prompt: What does asynchronous replication risk?

choices.label: Split brain on every write
Losing the latest writes if the leader fails before shipping them
Slower writes, because the leader waits for replicas
Replicas refusing reads

questions.explanation: Async is fast because it does not wait.

questions.prompt: What new problem does multi-leader replication bring?

choices.label: Conflicting writes on different leaders must be resolved
Every write needs a global lock
Reads can no longer scale
Replicas can no longer lag

questions.explanation: Two leaders can accept the same key at once.

questions.prompt: Order leader-follower replication.
questions.explanation: Replica reads lag by the shipping time.

questions.prompt: Replication for a payments ledger with a replica in another zone.
constraints: No committed payment may be lost
A few ms of extra write latency is fine

approaches.label: Synchronous replication
approaches.description: Leader waits for the replica

approaches.label: Asynchronous replication
approaches.description: Leader replies immediately

rationaleOptions.label: A commit is on two machines before success is returned
Synchronous replication makes writes faster
Losing a committed payment on failover is unacceptable

rationaleConflicts.r3: It makes them slower; the leader waits for the replica’s acknowledgement.

questions.explanation: Pay latency for durability where money is involved.

flashcards.back: Route a user’s reads to leader shortly after their writes.
Losing recent writes on failover.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Designing Distributed Systems

title: Quorums N/R/W
objectives: Use R + W > N to reason about reading the latest write
Tune N, R, W for read- or write-heavy loads
Explain sloppy quorums and hinted handoff

cards.title: Quorums in one line
cards.body: With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so at least one replica returns the newest value.

cards.body: N=3, W=2, R=2 is the balanced default. W=1, R=3 makes writes fast and reads slow; W=3, R=1 does the opposite but any replica outage blocks writes.

cards.body: Treating R + W > N as full linearizability. Sloppy quorums, clock-based conflict resolution and concurrent writes can still return surprising results.

cards.title: Three guarantees
cards.body: At-most-once: send and forget; a crash can lose a message but never duplicates it. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged; nothing is lost but duplicates happen. cards.body: A consumer processes a message, then crashes before committing its offset. On restart it reads the message again. Producers also resend after a lost acknowledgement.

title: Idempotency
objectives: Explain why retries cause duplicates

cards.title: Retries create duplicates
cards.body: Networks time out after the server already did the work. The client retries, and without protection a UPI payment is charged twice. At-least-once queues redeliver the same way.

cards.title: Idempotency keys
cards.body: The client sends a unique key (Idempotency-Key header). The server stores key → result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of repeating the action.

cards.title: A retried payment
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client sends POST /pay with key K” to “Server finds K, returns stored success”, via “Server charges, stores K → success”.
steps: Client sends POST /pay with key K
Server finds K, returns stored success

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Checking for the key and then writing in two separate steps. Two concurrent retries can both pass the check. Make the key insert and the action atomic, for example with a unique constraint.

cards.title: Naturally idempotent operations
cards.body: Setting a value (status = shipped) is idempotent: doing it twice leaves the same result. Adding or appending (balance += 100) is not. Turn the second kind into the first by recording a key or checking a version.

questions.prompt: A payment request timed out on the client, but the server had already charged the card. The client retries. What prevents a double charge?

choices.label: An idempotency key: the server returns the stored result
A longer client timeout

questions.explanation: The retry is recognised and answered from storage.

questions.prompt: Two identical retries arrive in the same millisecond. Which design is safe?

choices.label: Keep keys in each server’s memory
Accept both and reconcile at month end
Check whether the key exists, then charge, in two steps

title: 2PC & Saga
objectives: Explain two-phase commit and why it blocks

cards.title: Two-phase commit
cards.body: A coordinator asks every participant to prepare (lock and promise), then tells all to commit or all to abort. It gives atomicity across databases, but participants hold locks while waiting, and if the coordinator dies after prepare they are stuck.

cards.title: Sagas
cards.body: A saga splits the work into local transactions, one per service. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions (refund, release the seat). No global locks, but the system is briefly inconsistent.

cards.title: A trip booking saga
cards.body: 5 steps from “Reserve flight” to “Compensate: cancel flight”, via “Reserve hotel”.

cards.title: Choreography vs orchestration
cards.body: Choreography: each service reacts to the others’ events; no central brain, but the flow is hard to see. Orchestration: a coordinator calls each step and runs compensations; easier to follow and change.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Defaulting to 2PC across microservices. It ties every service’s availability together and holds locks across network calls. Prefer sagas unless you truly need atomic commit.

cards.title: The dual-write problem
cards.body: A service saves an order and then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. If it crashes between the two, the order exists but nobody hears about it; if the publish succeeds and the database write fails, consumers act on an order that does not exist.

cards.title: Transactional outbox

cards.title: What consensus solves
cards.body: Several nodes must agree on one ordered log of commands even when some crash. Raft and Paxos do this; etcd, Consul and ZooKeeper use them to hold config, locks and leader information.

cards.title: Raft in brief
cards.body: One leader accepts writes, appends them to its log and replicates them to followers. An entry is committed once a majority has stored it. If followers stop hearing heartbeats, one starts an election for a new term and wins with a majority of votes.

cards.title: Majorities and fault tolerance
cards.body: N nodes need a majority, floor(N/2) + 1, so they tolerate floor((N − 1)/2) failures: 3 nodes survive 1, 5 survive 2. Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Running consensus on 2 nodes, or putting a high-latency link in every write. Two nodes cannot lose one and keep a majority, and every commit waits for the slowest member of the majority.

cards.title: Gossip

cards.body: Instances come and go with autoscaling and deploys, so their addresses change. Callers need a live list of healthy instances for each service.

cards.title: Registries
cards.body: Instances register with a registry (Consul, etcd, Eureka) on start and send heartbeats; dead ones expire. In Kubernetes, a Service and its DNS name do this for you.

cards.title: Client-side vs server-side
cards.body: Client-side discovery: the caller asks the registry and picks an instance itself. Server-side: the caller hits a load balancer or DNS name, which picks for it. Server-side keeps clients simple.

cards.title: A call with discovery
cards.body: 5 steps from “Instance starts and registers” to “Caller calls one; dead instances expire from the list”, via “It sends heartbeats”.
steps: Caller calls one; dead instances expire from the list

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Hard-coding IPs in config, or caching lookups with no refresh. Deploys then send traffic to instances that no longer exist.

questions.prompt: Why do microservices need service discovery?

choices.label: To encrypt traffic between services
Instance addresses change with autoscaling and deploys
To store each service’s data
To version the APIs

questions.explanation: Callers need current, healthy addresses.

questions.prompt: An instance crashes without deregistering. How does the registry notice?

choices.label: Callers edit the registry by hand
The crashed instance sends a final message
It never notices
Its heartbeats stop and its entry expires

questions.explanation: Heartbeats plus expiry clean up dead entries.

questions.prompt: Which is server-side discovery?

choices.label: Every instance broadcasts its address to every caller
The caller hits a load balancer, which picks a healthy instance
The caller reads IPs from a config file
The caller queries Consul and picks an instance itself

questions.explanation: The picking happens outside the client.

questions.prompt: Order a call with discovery.
questions.explanation: Registration comes first.

questions.prompt: In Kubernetes, what gives you discovery out of the box?

choices.label: A ConfigMap of IP addresses
A Deployment’s replica count
A Service with a stable DNS name
A liveness probe

questions.explanation: The Service tracks ready pods behind one name.

flashcards.back: Its heartbeats stop and its entry expires. Heartbeats plus expiry clean up dead entries.

title: Timeouts/Retries/Circuit Breakers
objectives: Set timeouts that fit the caller’s deadline
Retry safely without multiplying load
Use circuit breakers and bulkheads to contain failures

cards.title: Timeouts
cards.body: Every outbound call needs a timeout shorter than the caller’s own deadline. Without one, threads wait forever on a hung dependency and the caller runs out of threads too.

cards.title: Retries
cards.body: Retry only idempotent operations, a few times, with exponential backoff and jitter. Retries at every layer multiply: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers is up to 27 calls.

cards.title: Circuit breakers
cards.body: Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: after too many failures, calls fail fast without trying. Half-open: after a cooldown, a few trial calls decide whether to close again.

cards.title: A breaker through an outage
cards.body: 5 steps from “Closed: calls flow” to “Trials succeed: closed again”, via “Failures pass the threshold”.

cards.title: Bulkheads
cards.body: Give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so a slow recommendations service cannot use up the pool checkout needs.

questions.prompt: After the cooldown, a circuit breaker enters:

choices.label: Half-open: a few trial calls
A retry storm
Closed: all calls flow at once
Open again, permanently

questions.explanation: Trials decide whether to close.

questions.prompt: Three layers each make up to 3 attempts. Worst case, how many calls reach the bottom service for one user request?
questions.formula: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3
questions.workedAnswer: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3 = 27 calls.
questions.explanation: Each attempt above triggers up to 3 below: 3^3 = 27 calls.

questions.prompt: A dependency hangs and no timeout is set. What happens to the caller?

choices.label: The operating system retries the call
Only one thread waits
The call fails fast automatically
Its threads pile up waiting until it cannot serve anyone

questions.explanation: Hung calls spread the outage upward.

questions.prompt: Order a breaker through an outage and recovery.
questions.explanation: Fail fast while it is down.

questions.prompt: Checkout calls a flaky recommendations service.

approaches.label: Retry many times with no timeout
approaches.description: Keep trying until it works

approaches.label: Timeout, circuit breaker and a default fallback, in its own pool
approaches.description: Contain the dependency

rationaleOptions.label: Failing fast while it is down keeps threads free
Checkout must not wait on an optional feature
More retries help the dependency recover faster

rationaleConflicts.r3: Extra retries add load to a struggling service and slow its recovery.

questions.explanation: Contain optional dependencies so they cannot take checkout down.

flashcards.front: After the cooldown, a circuit breaker enters:
flashcards.back: Half-open: a few trial calls. Trials decide whether to close.

flashcards.front: A dependency hangs and no timeout is set. What happens to the caller?
flashcards.back: Its threads pile up waiting until it cannot serve anyone. Hung calls spread the outage upward.

title: Logs/Metrics/Traces
objectives: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Track RED (rate, errors, duration) for services and USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) for resources. Correlate with a trace ID propagated through every hop.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Metrics show what, logs show details, traces show where across services.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Request gets trace ID” to “Dashboards & alerts”, via “Each service logs it”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Logging everything at DEBUG in production with no structure or sampling.

questions.prompt: Best tool to find which of 8 services slowed down one request?

choices.label: A distributed trace
Error-rate metrics
A CPU dashboard
Grepping each service’s logs by timestamp

questions.explanation: Spans show time spent per hop.

questions.prompt: RED metrics for a service are:

choices.label: Rate, errors, duration
Retries, exceptions, deploys
Requests, events, disks
Reads, edits, deletes

questions.explanation: Service-level health in three numbers.

questions.prompt: Which is a USE metric for a database disk?

choices.label: Saturation, such as the I/O queue depth
Requests per second to the API
p99 checkout latency
Number of deploys

questions.explanation: USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources.

questions.prompt: Order how observability data flows.
questions.explanation: The trace id ties it together.

choices.label: Huge volume and cost, and hard to query
Metrics become inaccurate
Traces stop working
Logs become too short

questions.explanation: Structure and sample logs.

flashcards.back: Logs, metrics, traces.
99% of requests are faster than this.

title: Availability & SLAs
objectives: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year down, 99.99% ≈ 53 min/year. Components in series multiply availability (lower); redundant components in parallel raise it. SLO = internal target; SLA = contractual promise.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Availability is uptime percentage; each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Single node” to “Health checks + failover”, via “Find SPOFs”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Claiming five nines without redundancy across zones. Availability comes from removing single points of failure.

questions.prompt: Two services in series, each 99.9% available. End-to-end availability?

choices.label: About 99.8%

questions.explanation: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, assuming independent failures.

questions.prompt: Allowed downtime per year at 99.9% availability, in hours?
Two independent replicas, each 99% available, with instant failover. Availability?

choices.label: About 99.99%

questions.explanation: Both must fail: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999.

questions.prompt: SLO versus SLA?

choices.label: SLA is measured per request, SLO per year
SLO is the internal target; SLA is the promise to customers, with penalties
SLA is the internal target; SLO is the customer promise
They mean the same thing

questions.explanation: Set the SLO tighter than the SLA.

questions.prompt: Order the path to higher availability.
questions.explanation: Remove single points of failure step by step.

flashcards.back: ≈ 52.6 minutes.
Series multiplies (lower); parallel redundancy raises it.

title: Disaster Recovery & Multi-Region
objectives: Define RPO and RTO and derive them from business needs
Choose a disaster-recovery strategy
Explain the data cost of cross-region replication

cards.title: RPO and RTO
cards.body: RPO: how much data you can lose, measured in time (the last 5 minutes of writes). RTO: how long until service is back. Both are business decisions that set the design and the cost.

cards.title: Strategies
cards.body: Backup and restore: cheapest, hours of RTO. Pilot light: data replicated, minimal servers ready to scale. Warm standby: a smaller full copy running. Active-active: every region serves traffic; lowest RTO, hardest consistency.

cards.title: Regional failover
cards.body: 5 steps from “Mumbai region fails health checks” to “Fail back after the incident”, via “DNS or a global load balancer shifts traffic”.
steps: DNS or a global load balancer shifts traffic

cards.title: Data across regions
cards.body: Async replication between regions keeps writes fast but means RPO above zero: the last seconds of writes can be lost. Synchronous cross-region writes give RPO zero at tens of ms per write.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Never testing failover. Backups that were never restored and runbooks that were never run tend to fail on the day. Rehearse with game days.

questions.prompt: The business can lose at most 5 minutes of orders. Which number is this?

choices.label: An RTO of 5 minutes
An RPO of 5 minutes
A TTL of 5 minutes
An SLA of 5 minutes

questions.explanation: RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.

questions.prompt: Cheapest DR strategy when hours of RTO are acceptable?

choices.label: Backup and restore
Warm standby
Pilot light
Active-active

questions.explanation: Nothing runs until you need it.

questions.prompt: Order a regional failover.
questions.explanation: Promote data before scaling.

questions.prompt: Cross-region replication is asynchronous. Consequence on failover?

choices.label: The last seconds of writes may be lost (RPO above zero)
Every write gets slower by one round trip
Failover takes days
Reads become strongly consistent

questions.explanation: Async trades a small data-loss window for fast writes.

questions.prompt: DR for a payments app: RTO under 5 minutes, RPO near zero.
constraints: Writes can afford a few extra ms

approaches.label: Nightly backups
approaches.description: Restore when needed

approaches.label: Warm standby with synchronous replication to the nearby region
approaches.description: Running copy, no data lag

approaches.label: Async replication to a far region only
approaches.description: Fast writes

rationaleOptions.label: Synchronous replication keeps RPO at zero
Nightly backups meet a 5-minute RTO
A running standby can take traffic within minutes

rationaleConflicts.r3: Restoring from backups takes hours and loses up to a day of data.

questions.explanation: Targets drive the strategy.

flashcards.front: The business can lose at most 5 minutes of orders. Which number is this?
flashcards.back: An RPO of 5 minutes. RPO is data loss; RTO is downtime.

flashcards.front: Cheapest DR strategy when hours of RTO are acceptable?
flashcards.back: Backup and restore. Nothing runs until you need it.

flashcards.back: The last seconds of writes may be lost (RPO above zero). Async trades a small data-loss window for fast writes.

title: AuthN vs AuthZ
objectives: Prove who the user is: server sessions, signed tokens, or delegated OAuth/OIDC.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Sessions store state server-side (easy revoke). JWTs are signed, stateless, short-lived with refresh tokens. OAuth 2.0 delegates access; OIDC adds identity.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Prove who the user is: server sessions, signed tokens, or delegated OAuth/OIDC.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Login with OTP” to “Refresh when expired”, via “Verify”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Long-lived JWTs with no revocation path.

cards.title: Authentication vs authorization
cards.body: Authentication answers who you are (password, OTP, passkey, Sign in with Google). Authorization answers what you may do: can this user refund this order? Authenticate once per session; authorize on every request, close to the data.

questions.prompt: A logged-in support agent tries to refund an order from another region and is blocked. Which check stopped them?

choices.label: TLS
Rate limiting
Authorization
Authentication

questions.explanation: They proved who they are; they lacked permission for this action.

questions.prompt: Biggest drawback of long-lived stateless JWTs?

choices.label: They cannot be verified without the auth server
They require sticky sessions
They are hard to revoke before they expire
They are too small to carry claims

questions.explanation: Nothing server-side remembers them.

questions.prompt: Why might a bank prefer server-side sessions over JWTs?

choices.label: Sessions need no storage
A session can be revoked instantly by deleting it on the server
Sessions work without cookies
Every service verifies sessions without a lookup

questions.explanation: Server state makes revocation easy.

questions.prompt: Order a token-based login.

items.label: Call APIs with the access token

questions.explanation: Short access tokens, longer refresh tokens.

questions.prompt: Where should “can this user refund this order?” be checked?

choices.label: At the CDN
In the service that owns orders, on every request
Only in the app’s UI
Only at login

questions.explanation: UI checks are convenience; the service enforces.

flashcards.back: Long-lived token to get new short-lived access tokens.
Who you are vs what you can do.

title: OAuth 2.0 & OIDC
objectives: Separate OAuth 2.0 (authorization) from OIDC (authentication)
Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE
Choose token types for web and mobile

cards.title: Two jobs, two specs
cards.body: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act on your behalf with limited scopes (“read my Google Drive files”). OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top so the app also learns who you are: “Sign in with Google”.

cards.title: Code flow with PKCE
cards.body: The app redirects to the identity provider, gets a short-lived code back, and exchanges it, plus a PKCE verifier, for tokens over a back channel. PKCE stops a stolen code being redeemed by another app.

cards.title: Sign in with Google
cards.body: 4 steps from “App redirects to Google with code_challenge” to “App exchanges code + verifier for ID and access tokens”, via “User logs in and consents”.
steps: App redirects to Google with code_challenge
Google redirects back with a code
App exchanges code + verifier for ID and access tokens

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using an OAuth access token as proof of identity. It says what the app may do, not who the user is. Use the OIDC ID token for login.

questions.prompt: Why do mobile apps use PKCE?

choices.label: A stolen authorization code cannot be redeemed without the app’s secret verifier
It makes tokens last longer
It removes the need for HTTPS
It lets the app read the user’s password

questions.explanation: The verifier proves the redeemer started the flow.

questions.prompt: To log a user in with Google, which token proves who they are?

choices.label: The authorization code
The refresh token
The OAuth access token
The OIDC ID token

questions.explanation: Access tokens say what the app may do, not who the user is.

questions.prompt: An app asks to “read your Google Drive files”. What is this?

choices.label: OAuth 2.0 delegated access with a limited scope
Password sharing
A session cookie
OIDC login

questions.explanation: Scopes limit what the app can do on your behalf.

questions.prompt: Order “Sign in with Google” with PKCE.

items.label: App redirects to Google with a code challenge
Google redirects back with a code
App exchanges code + verifier for tokens

questions.explanation: Tokens come over the back channel.

questions.prompt: A fintech aggregator reads bank statements on a user’s behalf.
constraints: Users must be able to revoke access
The app should never see bank passwords

approaches.label: OAuth with scoped, revocable consent
approaches.description: Delegated access

approaches.label: Ask users for their bank password
approaches.description: Log in as them

rationaleOptions.label: The user grants limited, revocable access
Storing passwords is fine if they are encrypted
The app never handles the bank password

rationaleConflicts.r3: With the password the app can do anything as the user, and access cannot be scoped or revoked separately.

questions.explanation: Delegation beats impersonation.

flashcards.back: OAuth grants delegated access; OIDC adds identity via an ID token.
An intercepted authorization code being redeemed by another app.

flashcards.back: The OIDC ID token.

title: JWT
objectives: Explain what a JWT contains and who can read it
Weigh stateless tokens against revocation
Pick sensible token lifetimes

cards.title: Signed, not secret
cards.body: A JWT is header.payload.signature, base64-encoded. Anyone holding it can read the claims; the signature only proves they were not changed. Never put secrets in the payload.

cards.title: Why services like it
cards.body: Any service with the public key can verify a token without calling the auth server, so verification scales horizontally and survives an auth outage.

cards.title: Verifying a request
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client sends Authorization: Bearer token” to “Passes user claims to service”, via “Gateway checks signature with public key”.
steps: Gateway checks signature with public key

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Week-long access tokens. A stateless token cannot be easily revoked, so keep access tokens short (minutes) and use refresh tokens, which can be revoked server-side.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to put the user’s PAN in the JWT payload “because it is signed”. What is wrong?

choices.label: Anyone holding the token can decode it; signing only stops changes
Only the gateway can read the payload
The token becomes too large to sign
Nothing: signed tokens are encrypted

questions.explanation: Signed, not secret.

questions.prompt: A user logs out but their access token is valid for 7 more days. Which design limits this best?

choices.label: Make tokens valid for 30 days
Short-lived access tokens with revocable refresh tokens
Sign tokens twice
Store the token in localStorage

questions.explanation: Keep the window of a stolen token small.

questions.prompt: Why can 20 services verify JWTs without overloading the auth server?

choices.label: Each caches the auth database
The auth server pushes sessions to all of them
Each verifies the signature with the public key, without a call
Tokens are verified only at login

questions.explanation: Verification is local.

questions.prompt: Order JWT verification at the gateway.

items.label: Gateway checks the signature with the public key
Gateway checks exp, aud and iss
Gateway passes user claims to the service

questions.explanation: Signature first, then claims.

questions.prompt: Besides the signature, what should verification check?

choices.label: The token’s length
The client IP’s country
Expiry (exp), audience (aud) and issuer (iss)
The user’s password

questions.explanation: A valid signature on an expired or foreign token is still a reject.

flashcards.front: Can anyone read a JWT payload?
flashcards.back: Yes. It is signed, not encrypted.

flashcards.front: Why are JWTs easy to scale?
flashcards.back: Services verify them locally with a public key, no auth-server call.

flashcards.front: How do you limit damage from a stolen JWT?
flashcards.back: Short expiry plus revocable refresh tokens.

title: Security Essentials
objectives: Layer defences so one failure is not a breach
Prevent injection with parameterised queries
Handle secrets and permissions with least privilege

cards.title: Defence in depth
cards.body: Assume any one layer fails. Combine TLS in transit, authentication, authorization on every request, input validation, rate limits, encryption at rest and audit logs.

cards.title: Injection
cards.body: Never build SQL or shell commands from user input. Use parameterised queries, and validate input. One string-concatenated query can leak a whole table.

cards.title: Secrets
cards.body: Keep API keys and passwords out of code and images. Load them from a secrets manager at runtime, scope each to one service, and rotate them.

cards.title: A request through the layers
cards.body: 5 steps from “TLS at the edge” to “Validate input and run a parameterised query”, via “Rate limit and web firewall”.
steps: Validate input and run a parameterised query

cards.title: Least privilege
cards.body: Give each service and person only the access they need: a read-only database user for reporting, a bucket policy for one prefix. A breach then exposes less.

questions.prompt: Search builds SQL as "… WHERE name = '" + input + "'". Fix?

choices.label: Hide database error messages
Use a parameterised query
Wrap the same concatenation in a stored procedure
Strip quotes from the input with a regex

questions.explanation: Parameters keep data from being parsed as SQL.

questions.prompt: Where should a payment-gateway API key live?

choices.label: In a private Git repository
In the mobile app’s code
In a secrets manager, loaded at runtime and rotated
Baked into the Docker image

questions.explanation: Code and images get copied; secrets must not travel with them.

questions.prompt: The reporting service only reads orders. Its database user should have:

choices.label: Read-only access to the tables it needs
The admin account, for simplicity
Write access in case it needs it later
The same account as checkout

questions.explanation: Limit what a compromise can do.

questions.prompt: Order the layers a request passes through.
questions.explanation: Each layer catches what the previous missed.

questions.prompt: HTTPS is enabled everywhere. Is the API secure?

choices.label: Not by itself: you still need authentication, authorization, validation and rate limits
Yes, once the CDN is enabled
Yes, as long as certificates are renewed
Yes: TLS covers every attack

questions.explanation: TLS is one layer of several.

flashcards.back: Use a parameterised query. Parameters keep data from being parsed as SQL.

flashcards.front: The reporting service only reads orders. Its database user should have:
flashcards.back: Read-only access to the tables it needs. Limit what a compromise can do.

In the CDN configuration

title: HDFS
objectives: Describe the NameNode/DataNode split
Explain block replication and rack awareness
Know where HDFS fits and where it does not

cards.title: Big files, big blocks
cards.body: HDFS stores huge files split into large blocks (128 MB by default) across many DataNodes. One NameNode keeps the metadata: which blocks make up a file and where they live.

cards.title: Replication
cards.body: Each block is stored three times by default, with copies on different racks so a rack power failure does not lose data. Lost replicas are re-copied automatically.

cards.title: Reading a file
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client asks NameNode for block locations” to “NameNode never touches the data”, via “NameNode returns DataNodes per block”.
steps: Client asks NameNode for block locations
Client streams blocks directly from DataNodes

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using HDFS for millions of tiny files or low-latency lookups. Each file costs NameNode memory, and HDFS is built for large sequential scans, not serving user requests.

questions.prompt: Why are HDFS replicas placed on different racks?

choices.label: Because DataNodes cannot share a rack
To make writes faster
To use less storage
So one rack failure (power, switch) does not lose every copy

questions.explanation: Spread copies across failure domains.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a poor fit for HDFS?

choices.label: Scanning 50 TB of logs every night
Large Parquet files for Spark jobs
Millions of tiny files served to users with low latency
Archiving raw clickstream for batch jobs

questions.explanation: Every file costs NameNode memory, and HDFS is built for big scans.

questions.prompt: Order an HDFS read.

items.label: Client asks the NameNode for block locations
Data never passes through the NameNode

questions.explanation: The NameNode only handles metadata.

questions.prompt: What does the NameNode store?

choices.label: User passwords
Only the newest blocks
Metadata: which blocks make up each file and where they live
The file data itself

questions.explanation: DataNodes store the blocks.

questions.prompt: A 1,024 MB file in 128 MB blocks with 3× replication. How many block replicas are stored?
questions.workedAnswer: 1,024 MB ÷ 128 MB = 8 blocks; 8 × 3 = 24 replicas.
questions.explanation: 1,024 MB ÷ 128 MB = 8 blocks; 8 × 3 = 24 replicas.

flashcards.back: Metadata: file to block mapping and block locations, not the data.
Three copies, spread across racks.
Large sequential batch reads, not tiny files or low-latency lookups.

title: Inverted Index & Elasticsearch
objectives: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: An inverted index maps terms → documents. Analysers tokenise, lowercase and stem. Keep the DB as source of truth and sync to the search cluster via CDC or events.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 6 steps from “Write to DB” to “ranked results”, via “CDC event”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using SQL LIKE "%term%" on millions of rows for search.

questions.prompt: Why not search with LIKE '%paneer%' on millions of rows?

choices.label: LIKE cannot match Hindi text
A leading wildcard cannot use an index, so every row is scanned
LIKE only matches uppercase text

title: MapReduce & Spark
objectives: Explain map, shuffle and reduce
Say why Spark beats MapReduce for multi-step jobs
Spot and fix skew in a shuffle

cards.title: MapReduce
cards.body: Map: each worker reads a chunk and emits key-value pairs, such as (word, 1). Shuffle: pairs with the same key go to the same reducer. Reduce: combine the values per key. Moving computation to the data beats moving data.

cards.title: Counting words
cards.body: 5 steps from “Split input into chunks” to “Write the results”, via “Map: emit (word, 1)”.

cards.title: Spark
cards.body: Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across steps instead of writing to disk after every MapReduce stage, so multi-step jobs and iterative ML run much faster. Lost partitions are recomputed from lineage.

cards.title: Shuffles are expensive
cards.body: The shuffle moves data across the network. A skewed key, such as one celebrity’s id, sends most data to one reducer, which runs for hours while the rest finish. Salt hot keys or pre-aggregate.

cards.title: Batch or stream?
cards.body: Batch jobs process a bounded dataset, such as yesterday’s orders, with high throughput and minutes-to-hours latency. Use streaming when decisions must happen in seconds.

questions.prompt: In a MapReduce word count, what happens in the shuffle?

choices.label: Each line is split into words
Input files are compressed
Pairs with the same word are sent to the same reducer
Counts are summed

questions.explanation: Grouping by key happens between map and reduce.

questions.prompt: Why is Spark faster than classic MapReduce for multi-step jobs?

choices.label: It runs on a single machine
It keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing to disk between steps
It never recomputes anything
It skips the shuffle

questions.explanation: Disk round trips between stages dominate MapReduce.

questions.prompt: Order a word-count job.
questions.explanation: Map, shuffle, reduce.

questions.prompt: A nightly job groups views by creator. One creator has 40% of all views, and one reducer runs for hours. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Salt the hot key or pre-aggregate on the map side.

Surge pricing every 30 seconds

questions.explanation: Bounded data, hours of acceptable latency.

title: Stream Processing

cards.title: Results while data flows
cards.body: Batch jobs answer questions about yesterday. Stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) update answers continuously, such as fraud scores within seconds of a UPI transaction.

cards.title: Windows
cards.body: Streams are unbounded, so you aggregate over windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) or session (gaps of inactivity). Use event time, when it happened, not processing time, when it arrived.

title: Geospatial Indexing
objectives: Explain geohash and quadtree indexing

cards.body: Computing distance to every restaurant in India per request is too slow. Geospatial indexes bucket locations into cells so a query only checks nearby cells.

cards.title: Geohash and quadtrees
cards.body: Geohash encodes lat/long into a string; a shared prefix means nearby. Quadtrees split space into four until each cell holds few points, so dense Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas get big ones.

title: Time-Series DBs
objectives: Recognise time-series workloads
Explain downsampling and retention
Avoid high-cardinality labels

cards.title: Append-heavy, time-ordered
cards.body: Metrics, sensor readings and prices arrive as timestamped points, mostly appended and read as ranges (last hour, last week). Time-series databases compress and index for exactly that.

cards.title: Retention and rollups
cards.body: Raw 10-second points for 7 days, 1-minute averages for 90 days, hourly for years. Downsampling keeps dashboards fast and storage bounded.

cards.title: A metric’s life

steps: Ingest appends to the current time block

cards.body: Putting user IDs or request IDs in labels. Every unique label combination is a new series, so cardinality explodes and memory with it.

choices.label: Compaction was turned off
user_id values are stored as long strings

title: Blue-Green/Canary/Feature Flags
objectives: Compare blue-green and canary releases
Use feature flags and kill switches safely
Keep schema changes rollback-safe

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.body: Run two full environments. Deploy to the idle one (green), test it, then switch the router from blue to green. Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the switch, and database changes must work for both.

cards.title: Canary
cards.body: Send a small share of traffic (1%, then 5%, 25%) to the new version and watch error rates and latency. Roll back automatically if they get worse. It catches problems only real traffic shows.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.body: Ship code dark and turn features on per user, region or percentage at runtime. Kill switches turn a broken feature off without a deploy. Remove flags once rolled out, or they pile up as untested paths.

cards.title: A canary rollout
cards.body: 5 steps from “Deploy v2 next to v1” to “Roll back if metrics worsen”, via “Route 1% of traffic to v2”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Shipping a schema change the old version cannot read, then rolling back. Make changes backward compatible: add the new column, switch code, remove the old column later.

questions.prompt: What does a canary release do?

Switches all traffic at once and rolls back if users complain
Deploys to every server at 2 AM

Point the router back to the old environment

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what a container packages
Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: 5 steps from “New image pushed” to “One old pod is removed, repeat”, via “Deployment creates a new pod”.
steps: One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

The readiness probe checks the database
The rolling update is too fast

choices.label: Schedules replacement pods on healthy nodes
Restarts the node

Moves traffic to another cluster

questions.explanation: Controllers restore the declared state.

questions.explanation: Old pods leave only after new ones are ready.

title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination
objectives: Explain why deep offsets are slow
Implement cursor pagination with a stable key
Pick offset or cursor for a given screen

cards.title: Offset pagination
cards.body: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 is simple and lets users jump to page 500, but the database still walks past 10,000 rows, and inserts shift pages so items repeat or vanish.

cards.title: Cursor pagination
cards.body: Return an opaque cursor (the last item’s sort key) and fetch WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor LIMIT 20. Each page is an index seek, and new inserts do not shift what comes next. There is no jumping to page 500.

cards.title: Paging a feed with cursors

steps: Server seeks past it using the index
Repeat until there is no cursor

cards.title: A stable sort key
cards.body: Cursors need a unique, ordered key. created_at alone can tie, so use (created_at, id), with an index on that pair.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed. Deep pages get slower and new posts push items onto the next page, so users see duplicates.

The response contains 100,000 rows
It locks the table

created_at alone

title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
objectives: Contrast optimistic and pessimistic locking
Pick one based on contention

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention
cards.body: Low contention (editing your own profile): optimistic, no waiting. High contention on one row (the last Tatkal seat): pessimistic or atomic updates, because optimistic retries would mostly fail.

cards.title: Optimistic update
cards.body: 4 steps from “Read row with version 7” to “0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry”, via “Compute new value”.
steps: 0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external payment API. The lock lives for seconds and everything else queues behind it. Keep lock scopes short.

cards.title: The brief
cards.body: Boss 75 · URL Shortener: A bit.ly for SMS links sent by Indian banks and e-commerce apps. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 75 risks: Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

Friend requests

questions.explanation: In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry. Out of scope for this interview: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration; Video upload; Friend requests.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for URL Shortener?

choices.label: Redirect short link to original
Optional custom alias & expiry
Redirect p99 < 50 ms
Video upload

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Redirect p99 < 50 ms; 100:1 read/write; Links never collide. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener: assume 50M daily users each doing about 2 redirects a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak redirects per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Create short link from long URL” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for URL Shortener jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does URL Shortener need for reliability?

choices.label: Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids).

questions.explanation: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener must create short link from long URL while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

rationaleOptions.label: User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

cards.title: Quality bar

cards.title: Reference sketch

cards.title: Failure modes
cards.body: Boss 83 risks: Trips in SQL; surge via stream processing.

cards.body: Boss 83 close: peak QPS for Twitter/X, required components client, lb, websocket, service, queue, and one mitigation.

choices.label: Follow other users
Read a home timeline
Payroll
Timeline loads in under 200 ms

questions.prompt: Twitter/X: assume 200M daily users each doing about 50 timeline reads a day, with traffic peaking at 3× the daily average. Estimate peak timeline reads per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 200M × 50 = 10B timeline reads/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 120,000/s on average; × 3 peak ≈ 350,000/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 200M × 50 = 10B timeline reads/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 120,000/s on average; × 3 peak ≈ 350,000/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Post a short tweet” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for Twitter/X jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Twitter/X need for reliability?

choices.label: Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Fan-out on write for most users, read-time merge for celebrities.

questions.explanation: Fan-out on write for most users, read-time merge for celebrities. Timelines cached in memory per user. Fan-out workers are idempotent so redelivery does not duplicate tweets. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

rationaleOptions.label: Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
A queue removes the need to watch backlog

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “View shows & seat map” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for BookMyShow jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does BookMyShow need for reliability?

choices.label: Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Seat holds via conditional update or short Redis lock with TTL.
Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails

questions.explanation: Seat holds via conditional update or short Redis lock with TTL. Payment saga releases hold on failure/timeout. Virtual waiting room queue for blockbuster drops. questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the first version of Search Engine?

choices.label: Keyword search
Rides
Live chat

questions.explanation: In scope: Keyword search; Filters & facets; Ranking. Out of scope for this interview: Building custom hardware; On-prem mainframe integration; Live chat; Rides.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for Search Engine?

choices.label: Live chat
Results < 200 ms
Ranking
Filters & facets

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Results < 200 ms; Index updates within a minute; Scale for sales. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: Search Engine: assume 80M daily users each doing about 10 searches a day, with traffic peaking at 6× the daily average. Estimate peak searches per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 80M × 10 = 800M searches/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 9,300/s on average; × 6 peak ≈ 56,000/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 80M × 10 = 800M searches/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 9,300/s on average; × 6 peak ≈ 56,000/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Keyword search” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for Search Engine jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Search Engine need for reliability?

choices.label: Catalogue in SQL, synced via CDC events to Elasticsearch.
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low
Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails

questions.explanation: Catalogue in SQL, synced via CDC events to Elasticsearch. Facets and ranking in search cluster; cache hot queries. Sharded indices with replicas. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: Search Engine must keyword search while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

rationaleOptions.label: User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

choices.label: Thumbnails
Consume with offsets

questions.prompt: Distributed Message Queue: assume about 10B messages a day, with traffic peaking at 2× the daily average. Estimate peak messages per second.
questions.workedAnswer: 10B messages/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 120,000/s on average; × 2 peak ≈ 230,000/s.
questions.explanation: Average first, then apply the peak factor. 10B messages/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 120,000/s on average; × 2 peak ≈ 230,000/s. Anything within about 50% shows the right order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: A mobile client times out on “Produce messages” and retries. How do you stop the action happening twice?

choices.label: Switch the endpoint to GET so repeating it is harmless
Send an idempotency key; the server stores the result for that key and returns it on retry
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate
Raise the client timeout so retries never happen

questions.explanation: Timeouts can fire after the server already did the work, and TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart. An application-level idempotency key identifies the retry.

questions.prompt: Traffic for Distributed Message Queue jumps 10× and there is no cache or replica yet. Which component saturates first?
questions.explanation: Stateless app servers scale out behind the load balancer; a single primary store does not. Relieve it with caching or read replicas for reads, and partitioning or queues for writes.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Distributed Message Queue need for reliability?

choices.label: Scale the app tier vertically so a single large server never fails
Partitioned append-only segments on disk, replicated with leader/followers.
Retry failed writes immediately in a tight loop until they succeed
Acknowledge the write before it reaches durable storage to keep latency low

questions.explanation: Partitioned append-only segments on disk, replicated with leader/followers. Metadata/leadership via Raft. Consumer groups track offsets. The others are tempting but wrong: one big server is still a single point of failure, tight retry loops amplify an outage, and acknowledging before a durable write loses data on a crash.

questions.prompt: Distributed Message Queue must produce messages while side effects (notifications, analytics, indexing) also happen. How should the request be structured?

approaches.label: Everything synchronous
approaches.description: The request waits for every downstream call.

approaches.label: Everything asynchronous
approaches.description: Acknowledge immediately, do all work later, including the core write.

approaches.label: Synchronous critical path, queue for side effects
approaches.description: Do only what the user must wait for, publish the rest as events.

rationaleOptions.label: A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
A queue removes the need to watch backlog
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent or they will repeat side effects.
rationaleConflicts.r4: If consumers fall behind the backlog grows; you still need lag alerts, autoscaling and dead-letter queues.

questions.explanation: Keep the core write synchronous so the user gets a truthful answer, and move side effects behind a queue. Queues bring their own duties: duplicates, retries, ordering and backlog.

rationaleOptions.label: A queue delivers exactly once, so consumers need no idempotency
User-facing latency only includes the steps the user needs
Side effects can retry from the queue without failing the request

title: Clarifying Requirements
objectives: Separate functional from non-functional requirements
Ask the questions that change the design
State assumptions when answers are vague

cards.title: Functional first
cards.body: Ask what users do: the three or four core actions, such as post, follow and view the feed. Say out loud what is out of scope.

cards.title: Non-functional next
cards.body: Scale (users, QPS, data), latency targets, availability, consistency needs and the read/write ratio. These shape the architecture more than features do.

cards.title: Five clarifying minutes
cards.body: 5 steps from “Who are the users and what do they do?” to “State assumptions out loud”, via “Which features are core and which are later?”.
steps: Who are the users and what do they do?
Which features are core and which are later?

cards.title: India-scale anchors
cards.body: Useful anchors: about 900M internet users, UPI in the tens of billions of transactions a month, IPL streams with tens of millions of concurrent viewers. Use them to sanity-check numbers.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Asking twenty questions without stating assumptions, or asking none. Ask what changes the design, then say “I’ll assume X; tell me if that is off.”

choices.label: 500M daily users

Users can post photos and follow others
99.95% availability

choices.label: Do we support stories?
Can users tag friends?

Can users add filters?

choices.label: State an assumption, such as 100M daily users, and continue
Refuse to continue without a number
Skip estimation entirely
Design for unlimited scale

title: Deep Dives & Trade-off Language
objectives: Choose the part of the design worth a deep dive
Phrase trade-offs with requirement, cost and mitigation
Avoid absolute claims

cards.title: Choosing the deep dive
cards.body: Pick the part most likely to break at your numbers: the hot key, the write path, the fan-out. Or ask which part the interviewer wants. Go deep on one, not shallow on five.

cards.title: Trade-off sentences
cards.body: Use: “A or B. I choose A because requirement X; the cost is Y; I’ll mitigate with Z.” It shows judgement instead of memorised answers.

cards.title: A deep dive
cards.body: 5 steps from “Name the risk with a number” to “Say how you would monitor it”, via “Show how the design fails”.
steps: Name the risk with a number
Pick one and name its cost
Say how you would monitor it

cards.title: Soften absolutes
cards.body: Avoid “always” and “never”. Say “for this read-heavy feed I’d cache with a short TTL”, not “caching is always right”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Presenting one option as obviously correct with no downside. Interviewers push back until you name the cost; naming it first earns the point.

choices.label: Async replication is always better

Either works; it does not matter

questions.prompt: Order the trade-off sentence.
questions.explanation: The cost and mitigation are what interviewers listen for.

cards.title: Designing before scoping
cards.body: Drawing boxes before knowing scale or features. Everything after rests on guesses.

cards.title: Over-engineering
cards.body: Kafka, microservices and sharding for 1,000 users. Start simple and add components when a number forces you.

cards.title: Unused numbers
cards.body: Estimating, then never using the estimate. If you computed 50K QPS, say what it means for caching and the database.

cards.title: Silent thinking

title: Numbers & Latency Cheat Sheet
objectives: Recall the latency ladder by order of magnitude
Convert daily volumes to per-second rates
Size a server fleet from peak QPS

cards.title: Latency ladder
cards.body: Memory read: about 100 ns. SSD random read: about 100 µs. Same-datacentre round trip: about 0.5 ms. Disk seek: about 10 ms. Mumbai to Singapore: about 60 ms. India to US East: about 200 ms.

cards.title: Throughput anchors
cards.body: A tuned app server handles roughly 1–10K simple requests/s; a single Postgres primary a few thousand writes/s; Redis around 100K operations/s per node. Rough, but enough to size a fleet.

cards.title: Powers of ten
cards.body: A day is 86,400 s, about 10^5. A million a day is about 12 a second; a billion a day is about 12K a second. A million 1 KB records is about 1 GB; a million 1 MB files is about 1 TB.

cards.title: Sizing a fleet
cards.body: 5 steps from “Peak QPS from the estimate” to “Add N+1 for failures”, via “Per-server capacity from the anchors”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Quoting numbers to three significant figures. Interviewers want orders of magnitude and stated assumptions, not false precision.

title: Pattern-to-Use-Case Map
objectives: Map workload shapes to standard patterns
Pick patterns for read-heavy, write-heavy, real-time and correctness-first features
Link each pattern back to its lesson

cards.title: Read-heavy
cards.body: Cache-aside, a CDN for static files and media, read replicas. Examples: product pages, news feeds, URL redirects.

cards.title: Write-heavy and spiky
cards.body: Queues to absorb bursts, batching, LSM or wide-column stores, sharding by a high-cardinality key. Examples: logging, IoT, clickstreams.

cards.title: Real-time
cards.body: WebSockets or SSE through gateways, pub/sub to route messages, presence in Redis. Examples: chat, live scores, ride tracking.

cards.title: Correctness first
cards.body: Transactions, idempotency keys, sagas, strong consistency on the hot rows. Examples: payments, bookings, inventory.

cards.title: Search and nearby
cards.body: An inverted index for text, geohash or a quadtree for location, both fed from the primary database by CDC. Examples: product search, restaurants near me.
